title: Relational databases and SQL flash cards

cards.front: What is a database?
back: An organised collection of data.

cards.front: What is one row of a database table called?
back: Record.

cards.front: What is one column of a database table called?
back: Field.

cards.front: Which key uniquely identifies each record in a table?
back: Primary key.

cards.front: Which key can link a record to a primary key in another table?
back: Foreign key.

cards.front: Which SQL keyword sorts the rows in a result?
back: ORDER BY.

cards.front: Which SQL symbol selects all fields?
Name a suitable data type for the whole-number field YearGroup.
back: Integer.

cards.front: Name a suitable data type for a person's name.
back: Text/string.

cards.front: Explain a relational database.
back: It stores data in **related tables**.
Tables can be linked by matching a foreign key to a primary key.

cards.front: Explain why a person's name is usually a poor primary key.
back: Different people can have the same name.
A primary key must identify each record uniquely, so a unique ID is more suitable.

cards.front: In Pupils(PupilID, Name) and Loans(LoanID, PupilID, BookTitle), identify the primary key of Loans and its foreign key.
back: **Primary key:** LoanID.
**Foreign key:** PupilID, linking to the pupil identified in Pupils.

cards.front: Explain why the same PupilID may appear in several Loan records.
back: One pupil may borrow several books.
Each loan has a unique LoanID but uses the same foreign key to identify that pupil.

cards.front: Explain the difference between data redundancy and data inconsistency.
back: **Redundancy** is unnecessary duplication of data.
**Inconsistency** occurs when copies disagree, for example two different addresses for the same pupil.

cards.front: The table Pupils has fields PupilID, Name and YearGroup. Write SQL to display only Name and YearGroup for every pupil.
back:
```sql
SELECT Name, YearGroup
FROM Pupils;
```

cards.front: Pupils has a field YearGroup. Write SQL to return all fields for pupils in Year 10.
back:
```sql
SELECT *
FROM Pupils
WHERE YearGroup = 10;
```

cards.front: Pupils has fields PupilID and Name. Write SQL to list the names in alphabetical order.
back:
```sql
SELECT Name
FROM Pupils
ORDER BY Name ASC;
```

cards.front:
Pupils contains Shreya in Year 10, Amir in Year 11 and Mia in Year 10. What names are returned by this query?
```sql
SELECT Name
FROM Pupils
WHERE YearGroup = 10
ORDER BY Name DESC;
```
back: Shreya, then Mia.

cards.front: Explain how linking a pupil table to a loan table can reduce inconsistency.
back: Store the pupil's name once in the pupil table.
Each loan stores the **PupilID foreign key**, rather than another copy of the name.
A name change is made in one record, avoiding conflicting copies in different loan records.

cards.front: Pupils has fields PupilID, Name and YearGroup. Write SQL to select names in Years 10 or 11.
back:
```sql
SELECT Name
FROM Pupils
WHERE YearGroup = 10 OR YearGroup = 11;
```

cards.front: Loans has fields LoanID, PupilID, BookTitle and DaysLoaned. Write SQL to return BookTitle for loans lasting at least 14 days but no more than 21 days.
back:
```sql
SELECT BookTitle
FROM Loans
WHERE DaysLoaned >= 14 AND DaysLoaned <= 21;
```

cards.front: Explain why this condition cannot match any record: YearGroup = 10 AND YearGroup = 11.
back: One record has one value for YearGroup.
**AND** requires both conditions to be true, but that value cannot be both 10 and 11.
Use **OR** to match either year group.

cards.front: Pupils has fields PupilID, Name and YearGroup. Insert pupil 104, named Lena, in Year 11.
back:
```sql
INSERT INTO Pupils (PupilID, Name, YearGroup)
VALUES (104, 'Lena', 11);
```

cards.front: Pupils has fields PupilID, Name and YearGroup. Change pupil 101's YearGroup to 11.
back:
```sql
UPDATE Pupils
SET YearGroup = 11
WHERE PupilID = 101;
```

cards.front: Loans has a primary key LoanID. Write SQL to delete only loan 502.
back:
```sql
DELETE FROM Loans
WHERE LoanID = 502;
```

cards.front:
An administrator runs this query by mistake. Explain its effect and show a corrected version that affects only pupil 101.
```sql
UPDATE Pupils
SET YearGroup = 11;
```
back: The missing **WHERE** means every record is updated, so all pupils are assigned Year 11. A condition using the unique primary key limits the change to the intended pupil.

```sql
UPDATE Pupils
SET YearGroup = 11
WHERE PupilID = 101;
```

cards.front: Loans has fields LoanID, PupilID, BookTitle and DaysLoaned. Write SQL to show BookTitle and DaysLoaned for loans longer than 7 days, longest first.
back:
```sql
SELECT BookTitle, DaysLoaned
FROM Loans
WHERE DaysLoaned > 7
ORDER BY DaysLoaned DESC;
```

cards.front: A pupil table has records (101, Shreya), (102, Amir), (103, Mia). A loan table has matching PupilID values 101, 101 and 102. Describe the rows produced by matching Pupils.PupilID to Loans.PupilID, and explain why the match matters.
back: Shreya appears in **two matching rows**, one for each loan.
Amir appears in **one matching row**.
Mia has **no matching loan**, so does not appear in this matching result.
Matching the keys links each loan to the correct pupil; without a linking condition, unrelated pupil and loan rows could be combined.
